'''''Chlorophytum comosum''''', usually called '''spider plant''' or '''common spider plant''' due to its spider-like look, also known as '''spider ivy''', '''airplane plant''',<ref name=Texasgardeners>{{cite web |url=https://txmg.org/hendersonmg/plant-library/airplane-plant-or-spider-plant/ |title=Airplane Plant or Spider Plant |website=txmg.org |access-date=2 March 2024 }}</ref> '''ribbon plant''' (a name it shares with ''[[Dracaena sanderiana]]''),<ref name=Poole1991/> and '''hen and chicks''',<ref name=Plantzafrica>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantcd/chlorophytcom.htm |title=Chlorophytum comosum |website=PlantZAfrica.com |date=November 2012 |author=Ernst van Jaarsveld |publisher=South African National Biodiversity Institute |access-date=27 June 2016 }}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[evergreen]] [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[flowering plant]] of the family [[Asparagaceae]]. It is [[native plant|native]] to [[Tropical Africa|tropical]] and Southern Africa but has become naturalized in other parts of the world, including [[Western Australia]] and Bangladesh.<ref name=KewWC>{{citation |title=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families |publisher=The Board of Trustees of the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/home.do |access-date=26 September 2011}}, search for "Chlorophytum comosum"</ref><ref>Howell, J.T., P.H. Raven & P. Rubtzoff. 1958. Flora of San Francisco. Wasmann J. Biology 16:1-155.</ref> ''Chlorophytum comosum'' is easy to grow as a [[houseplant]] because of its resilience, but it can be sensitive to the [[fluoride]] in tap water, which commonly gives it "burnt tips". [[Variegation|Variegated]] forms are the most popular.

== Description ==
''Chlorophytum comosum'' grows to about {{convert|60|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall, although as a hanging plant  it can descend many feet. It has fleshy, [[Tuber#Root tubers|tuberous roots]], each about {{convert|5|-|10|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long. The long narrow leaves reach a length of {{convert|20|-|45|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} and are around {{convert|6|-|25|mm|in|1}} wide.<ref name=McCuneHardin>{{citation |last1=McCune |first1=S. |last2=Hardin |first2=D. W. |name-list-style=amp |contribution=''Chlorophytum comosum'' (Thunb.) Jacques |title=PlantNET - The Plant Information Network System of The Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust |location=Sydney, Australia |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Chlorophytum~comosum |year=1994 |access-date=27 September 2011 }}</ref>

[[File:2006-12-09Chlorophytum07-03.jpg|thumb|175px|Flower of 'Vittatum']]
Flowers are produced in a long, branched [[inflorescence]], which can reach a length of up to {{convert|75|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} and eventually bends downward to meet the earth. Flowers initially occur in clusters of 1–6 at intervals along the stem ([[scape (botany)|scape]]) of the inflorescence. Each cluster is at the base of a [[bract]], which ranges from {{convert|2|-|8|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} in length, becoming smaller toward the end of the inflorescence. Most of the flowers that are produced initially die off, so that relatively, the inflorescences are sparsely flowered.<ref name=McCuneHardin/>

Individual flowers are greenish-white, borne on stalks ([[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s) some {{convert|4|-|8|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long. Each flower has six triply veined [[tepal]]s that are {{convert|6|-|9|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long and slightly hooded or boat-shaped at their tips. The [[stamen]]s consist of a [[pollen]]-producing anther about {{convert|3.5|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long with a filament of similar length or slightly longer. The central [[Style (botany)|style]] is {{convert|3|-|8|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long. Seeds are produced in a [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]], {{convert|3|-|8|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} long, on stalks (pedicels) that lengthen to up to {{convert|12|mm|in|1|abbr=on}}.<ref name=McCuneHardin/>

The inflorescences carry not only flowers but also vegetative [[plantlets]] at the tips of their branches, which eventually droop and touch the soil, developing [[adventitious root]]s. The stems (scapes) of the inflorescence are called "[[stolons]]" in some sources, but this term is more correctly used for stems that do not bear flowers and have roots at the [[Plant stem|nodes]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hickey |first1=M. |last2=King |first2=C. |title=The Cambridge Illustrated Glossary of Botanical Terms |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2001 }}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
The first formal description of ''Chlorophytum comosum'' was by the Swedish naturalist [[Carl Peter Thunberg]] as ''Anthericum comosum'' in the 1794 volume of ''Prodromus Plantarum Capensium'', Thunberg's work on the plants of South Africa.<ref name="IPNI1">{{IPNI|id=530288-1|title=Anthericum comosum Thunb., Prodr. Pl. Cap. 1: 63 (1794).|access-date=26 September 2011 }}</ref><ref name="Thunber 1794">Thunberg, Carl Peter. 1794. [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/3553183 ''Prodromus Plantarum Capensium''.] p. 63.</ref> The species was subsequently moved to a number of different genera, including ''Phalangium'', ''[[Caesia]]'', ''Hartwegia'' <small>Nees</small>, and ''Hollia'', before receiving its current placement in ''Chlorophytum'' by Jacques in 1862.<ref name=KewWC/>

The species has been confused with ''Chlorophytum capense'' <small>(L.) Voss</small> by some authors, but this is a different species.<ref name=GRIN/>

=== Intra-specific variation ===
[[File:2007-06-24Chlorophytum comosum04.jpg|thumb|175px|Fleshy roots of pot-grown plant]]
There are three described varieties of the species: the [[Autonym (botany)|autonym]] ''C. comosum'' var. ''comosum'' has strap-shaped narrow leaves and is found along forest margins; ''C. comosum'' var. ''bipindense'' has broader, [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]] leaves with stripes on the underside and the inflorescences are 2–3 times the length of the leaves; and ''C. comosum'' var. ''sparsiflorum'' also has broader leaves that narrow to the base, and usually lacks a petiole and the striping on the underside of the leaf and the inflorescences are up to two times the length of the leaves. The latter two are rainforest-dwelling taxa that had been described earlier as separate species, but botanists [[Axel Dalberg Poulsen]] and [[Inger Nordal]] reduced the taxa to varieties of ''C. comosum'' in 2005.<ref name="Poulsen & Nordal 2005">Poulsen, AD, and I Nordal. 2005. A phenetic analysis and revision of Guineo-Congolean rainforest taxa of ''Chlorophytum'' (Anthericaceae). ''Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society'', 148: 1-20.</ref>

Delimitation of species boundaries within the genus ''Chlorophytum'' is reported to be difficult, possibly because of several evolutionary radiations into forest environments that led to morphological aspects that are too similar to reliably distinguish separate species. The evidence given to support this is the widespread distribution of most taxa in the genus and poor seed dispersal, leading to the conclusion of deeper evolutionary divergence among the taxa. [[File:Chlorophytum comosum 01.jpg|thumb|'Variegatum']]

The three described [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] in ''C. comosum'' could be an example of this [[convergent evolution]] of leaf shape among the forest-dwelling varieties from species of disparate origin, leading to the species ''C. comosum'' being [[polyphyletic]], instead of the traditional view of morphological divergence among the varieties within the species with the assumption of a common origin ([[monophyly]]). The widespread ''C. comosum'' var. ''comosum'' has slender, near linear leaves that lack a petiole similar to plants found in cultivation and is only found growing at the margins of the rainforest. The two other varieties, ''C. comosum'' var. ''sparsiflorum'' and ''C. comosum'' var. ''bipindense'', possess petioles and have broader leaves necessary for collecting more light in the shady [[Guineo-Congolean rainforest]]. A study published in 2005 used 16 morphological characters and was unable to delimit species boundaries among these three taxa, so they were relegated to varietal status.<ref name="Poulsen & Nordal 2005" /> A follow-up study published in 2008 provided preliminary evidence from [[Phylogenetics|phylogenetic analysis]] of [[plastid]] and nuclear DNA sequences that established samples from disparate collections sites identified as ''C. comosum'' were [[polyphyletic]].<ref name="Bjora et al 2008">Bjorå, CS, A Hemp, G Hoell, and I Nordal. 2008. A taxonomic and ecological analysis of two forest ''Chlorophytum'' taxa (Anthericaceae) on Mount Kilimanjaro, Tanzania. ''Plant Systematics and Evolution'', 274: 243-253.</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Chlorophytum comosum'' has a widespread native distribution in Africa, being native to six of the ten [[World Geographical Scheme for Recording Plant Distributions]] regions of Africa (West Tropical Africa, West-Central Tropical Africa, Northeast Tropical Africa, East Tropical Africa, South Tropical Africa, and Southern Africa).<ref name="KewWC" />

== Cultivation ==
[[File:Chlorophytum comosum Ampel.jpg|thumb|'Variegatum' in a hanging basket showing the plantlets]]

''Chlorophytum comosum'' is a popular [[houseplant]]. The cultivars with all-green leaves forms only a small proportion of plants sold. More common are two variegated cultivars:<ref name=Poole1991>{{citation |last1=Poole |first1=R.T. |last2=Chase |first2=A.R. |last3=Osborne |first3=L.S. |year=1991 |title=Spider Plant Production Guide (CFREC-Apopka Foliage Plant Research Note RH-91-33) |publisher=Central Florida Research and Education Center, University of Florida |url=http://mrec.ifas.ufl.edu/foliage/folnotes/spider.htm |access-date=26 September 2011 |name-list-style=amp }}</ref>

* ''C. comosum'' 'Vittatum' has mid-green leaves with a broad central white stripe. It is often sold in [[hanging basket]]s to display the [[plantlet]]s.<ref name=Poole1991/> The long stems are white. There is also a "curly" version with this type of striping and compact size.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite web |url=https://plantcaretoday.com/spider-plant-care.html |title=Spider Plant Care: Growing Chlorophytum Comosum |website=plantcaretoday.com |access-date=17 April 2021 }}</ref> 
* ''C. comosum'' 'Variegatum' has darker green leaves with white margins. It is generally smaller than the previous cultivar. The long stems are green.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://indoormint.com/spider-plant-growing-long-stem/ |title=Spider Plant Growing Long Stem |website=indoormint.com |date=26 July 2021 }}</ref>
Both cultivars have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/91043/Chlorophytum-comosum-Variegatum-(v)/Details |title=Chlorophytum comosum 'Variegatum' (v) | variegated spider ivy/RHS Gardening }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/67933/Chlorophytum-comosum-Vittatum-(v)/Details |title=Chlorophytum comosum 'Vittatum' (v) | spider ivy 'Vittatum'/RHS Gardening }}</ref> (confirmed 2017).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |title=AGM Plants - Ornamental |date=July 2017 |page=18 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=24 January 2018 }}</ref>
In 2021, 17 other cultivars were listed, including 'Bonnie', 'Green Bonnie' and 'Hawaiian'.<ref name=Morr21>{{Citation |mode=cs1 |last1=Morris |first1=Mercy |date=2021 |title=Arachnophilia |journal=The Plant Review |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=22–27 }}</ref>

=== Propagation ===
[[File:SpiderPlantPlantlets.jpg|alt=A picture of a spider plant's plantlets and budding flowers.|thumb|Plantlets and budding flowers]] [[File:Семя хлорофитума хохлатого под микроскопом.jpg|alt=Microscope image of a seed.|thumb|Plant seed taken on a microscope]]
Propagating ''Chlorophytum comosum'' commonly occurs through [[Potting soil|potting]] the plantlets, informally referred to as 'spiderettes',<ref>{{cite web |title=StackPath |url=https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/houseplants/spider-plant/propagating-spiderettes.htm |access-date=13 November 2020 |website=www.gardeningknowhow.com |date=8 May 2015 }}</ref> or 'pups',<ref>{{Cite web |last=Almanac |first=Old Farmer's |title=Spider Plants |url=https://www.almanac.com/plant/spider-plants |access-date=13 November 2020 |website=Old Farmer's Almanac }}</ref> directly into potting soil, or pumice, attached to the main plant or cutting the running stems and then potting them.

Spider plants are easy to grow, being able to thrive in a wide range of conditions. They will tolerate temperatures down to {{convert|35|°F|°C|disp=flip}}, but grow best at temperatures between {{convert|65|°F|°C|disp=flip}} and {{convert|90|°F|°C|disp=flip}}. Plants can be damaged by high [[fluoride]] or [[boron]] levels.<ref name=Poole1991/>

== Toxicity and effects on pets ==
Spider plants are non-toxic to humans and pets,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/toxic-and-non-toxic-plants/spider-plant |title=Spider Plant |website=[[American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals]] (ASPCA) |access-date=17 April 2021 }}</ref> and are considered edible.<ref name="autogenerated1" />

== Air purification ==
The [[NASA Clean Air Study]] suggested that air plants were effective at removing common household air toxins [[formaldehyde]] and [[xylene]]; however, these results are not applicable to typical buildings, where outdoor-to-indoor air exchange already removes volatile organic compounds ([[Volatile Organic Compound|VOCs]]) at a rate that could only be matched by the placement of 10–1000 plants/m{{sup|2}} of a building's floor space.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cummings |first1=Bryan E. |last2=Waring |first2=Michael S. |title=Potted plants do not improve indoor air quality: a review and analysis of reported VOC removal efficiencies |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41370-019-0175-9 |journal=Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology |pages=253–261 |language=en |doi=10.1038/s41370-019-0175-9 |date=March 2020 |volume=30 |issue=2 |pmid=31695112 |s2cid=207911697 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The results also failed to replicate in future studies, with a 2014 review stating that:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dela Cruz |first1=M |last2=Christensen |first2=JH |last3=Thomsen |first3=JD |last4=Müller |first4=R |date=2014 |title=Can ornamental potted plants remove volatile organic compounds from indoor air? – a review |url=https://greenplantsforgreenbuildings.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Dela-Cruz-2014-review-on-phytoremediation-with-indoor-plants-2.pdf |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |volume=21 |issue=24 |pages=13909–13928 |doi=10.1007/s11356-014-3240-x |pmid=25056742 |s2cid=207272189 |access-date=15 August 2018 }}</ref>

{{Quote|While the plant's ability to take up VOCs is well documented in laboratory studies, the effect of plants on indoor air in complex environments like offices requires further investigations to clarify the full capacity of plants in real-life settings.}}

In the laboratory settings used in the Clean Air Study, spider plants were shown to reduce formaldehyde pollution, and approximately 70 plants would neutralize the formaldehyde released by materials in a representative (c. {{cvt|167|m2|disp=sqbr}}) [[Green building|energy-efficient house]], assuming each plant occupies a {{cvt|3.8|L}} pot.<ref name="nasastudy">{{cite journal |author1=Wolverton, B. C. |author2=McDonald, Rebecca C. |author3=Watkins, E. A. |date=1984 |url=http://www.greenenergyhelps.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/Wolverton-et-al-1984.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150427225702/http://www.greenenergyhelps.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/Wolverton-et-al-1984.pdf |archive-date=27 April 2015 |title=Foliage plants for removing indoor air pollutants from energy-efficient homes |journal=Economic Botany |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=224–228 |doi=10.1007/BF02858837 |hdl=2060/19860066312 |s2cid=41933312 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Edibility==
The tuberous roots are reportedly edible (whether raw or cooked unstated) although mild [[laxative]] effects are claimed by the [[Nguni people]] of its native South Africa.<ref name= "stuartexchange"/>
